html:
The Valdivia culture lived on the coast of Ecuador from about 3800 to 1500 BCE. It made some of the oldest pottery in the Americas. The map shows it from 3000 to 2000 BCE. (It has nothing to do with the city of Valdivia in Chile.)

Valdivia people lived in settled villages. At Real Alto, one of the best known sites, oval houses stood in rings around a central plaza. They fished, gathered shellfish, and grew crops that probably included maize, beans, squash and cotton, one of the earliest farming peoples of South America.

They are famous for small clay figurines of women, the "Venus" figures, perhaps used in ritual. In the 1960s the archaeologists Emilio Estrada, Betty Meggers and Clifford Evans suggested that Valdivia pottery came from fishermen of the Jōmon culture of Japan drifting across the Pacific. Few accept this now; the pottery is seen as a local invention. Valdivia was followed by the Machalilla culture, and its people are part of the deep background of the later Chavín world.
